calibration.statement: The Pacific Ocean covers a greater surface area than all of Earth's land combined.
calibration.note: Pacific surface is about 165 million km2; total land is about 149 million km2.

calibration.statement: The summit of Mount Everest is the point on Earth's surface farthest from the planet's centre.
calibration.note: Chimborazo in Ecuador is farther out, because the Earth bulges at the equator.

calibration.statement: Alaska has more coastline than all other US states combined.
calibration.note: Alaska's tidal shoreline is roughly 54,000 km, more than the rest of the country together.

calibration.statement: The Sahara is the largest hot desert in the world.
calibration.note: About 9.2 million km2. Antarctica is a larger desert overall, but it is a cold one.

calibration.statement: Mount Kilimanjaro is located in Kenya.
calibration.note: It is in Tanzania, close to the Kenyan border.

calibration.statement: Reno, Nevada lies farther west than Los Angeles, California.
calibration.note: Reno is near 119.8 degrees west; Los Angeles is near 118.2 degrees west.

calibration.statement: Istanbul lies on two continents.
calibration.note: The Bosphorus divides its European and Asian sides.

calibration.statement: The whole of Africa lies within the Eastern Hemisphere.
calibration.note: The prime meridian crosses West Africa, so parts of Ghana, Mali and others sit west of it.

calibration.statement: Russia shares a land border with North Korea.
calibration.note: A short border of about 17 km along the Tumen River.

calibration.statement: The shore of the Dead Sea is the lowest exposed land elevation on Earth.
calibration.note: More than 400 metres below sea level.

calibration.statement: Vatican City is the smallest sovereign state in the world by area.
calibration.note: About 0.49 km2.

calibration.statement: Iceland has a larger population than Malta.
calibration.note: Iceland is around 390,000 people; Malta is over 500,000 in a far smaller area.

calibration.statement: More people live in the Tokyo metropolitan area than in the whole of Australia.
calibration.note: Greater Tokyo is around 37 million; Australia is around 26 million.

calibration.statement: Australia is wider from east to west than the contiguous United States.
calibration.note: Australia spans roughly 4,000 km; the contiguous US spans roughly 4,300 km.

calibration.statement: Light takes more than one second to travel from the Moon to the Earth.
calibration.note: About 1.28 seconds at the mean distance.

calibration.statement: Venus is the hottest planet in the Solar System.
calibration.note: Surface near 465 C, hotter than Mercury despite being farther from the Sun.

calibration.statement: A day on Venus is longer than a year on Venus.
calibration.note: It rotates in about 243 Earth days and orbits in about 225.

calibration.statement: Saturn is the only planet in the Solar System with a ring system.
calibration.note: Jupiter, Uranus and Neptune all have rings, they are simply much fainter.

calibration.statement: Helium was detected on the Sun before it was found on Earth.
calibration.note: Identified in the solar spectrum in 1868, isolated on Earth in 1895.

calibration.statement: Pure water is a good conductor of electricity.
calibration.note: Pure water is a poor conductor. Dissolved ions do the conducting in ordinary water.

calibration.statement: Sound travels faster through water than through air.
calibration.note: About 1,480 m/s in water against about 343 m/s in air.

calibration.statement: Window glass is a liquid that slowly flows at room temperature.
calibration.note: It is an amorphous solid. Old uneven panes come from the way they were made.

calibration.statement: Lightning never strikes the same place twice.
calibration.note: Tall structures are struck repeatedly. The Empire State Building is hit many times a year.

calibration.statement: The Coriolis effect determines the direction water swirls when a household sink drains.
calibration.note: At that scale basin shape and initial motion dominate completely.

calibration.statement: Oxygen is the most abundant element by mass in the Earth's crust.
calibration.note: Roughly 46 percent, mostly locked in silicate and oxide minerals.

calibration.statement: Diamond is the hardest naturally occurring material known.
calibration.note: It sits at the top of the Mohs scale.

calibration.statement: Human beings normally have more than 23 pairs of chromosomes.
calibration.note: Exactly 23 pairs, 46 chromosomes in total.

calibration.statement: Bananas are measurably radioactive.
calibration.note: They contain potassium, and a fixed fraction of natural potassium is potassium-40.

calibration.statement: Bats are blind.
calibration.note: All bat species can see. Many also use echolocation.

calibration.statement: Sharks existed before trees did.
calibration.note: Sharks appear around 450 million years ago; the first trees around 390 million.

calibration.statement: An octopus has three hearts.
calibration.note: Two branchial hearts serve the gills and one systemic heart serves the body.

calibration.statement: Human blood is blue inside the body and turns red on contact with air.
calibration.note: Human blood is always red. Deoxygenated blood is a darker red.

calibration.statement: Goldfish have a memory span of only a few seconds.
calibration.note: They can be trained on tasks and retain them for months.

calibration.statement: Antibiotics are effective treatments for viral infections such as the common cold.
calibration.note: Antibiotics act on bacteria. They do nothing to viruses.

calibration.statement: A human body contains at least as many bacterial cells as human cells.
calibration.note: Current estimates put the ratio near one to one, slightly favouring bacteria.

calibration.statement: The human brain accounts for roughly a fifth of the body's resting energy use.
calibration.note: About 20 percent, from roughly 2 percent of body mass.

calibration.statement: Humans use only about ten percent of their brains.
calibration.note: Imaging shows activity throughout the brain. The claim has no basis.

calibration.statement: Bulls become enraged by the colour red.
calibration.note: Cattle are red-green colour blind. It is the movement of the cape that provokes them.

calibration.statement: Cleopatra lived closer in time to the first Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid of Giza.
calibration.note: The Great Pyramid is around 2560 BC; Cleopatra died in 30 BC; the landing was 1969.

calibration.statement: The Western Roman Empire fell before teaching began at Oxford.
calibration.note: 476 AD against evidence of teaching at Oxford from 1096.

calibration.statement: Harvard University was founded before calculus was developed.
calibration.note: Harvard was chartered in 1636; Newton and Leibniz worked in the 1660s to 1680s.

calibration.statement: A working fax machine was patented before the American Civil War began.
calibration.note: Alexander Bain patented an electric printing telegraph in 1843.

calibration.statement: Nintendo was founded before the Ottoman Empire ended.
calibration.note: Nintendo began in 1889 as a playing card maker; the Ottoman Empire ended in 1922.

calibration.statement: Anne Frank and Martin Luther King Jr. were born in the same year.
calibration.note: Both were born in 1929.

calibration.statement: Napoleon Bonaparte was unusually short for a Frenchman of his era.
calibration.note: He was about 1.68 m, close to average. The myth comes from differing inch measures and British caricature.

calibration.statement: The Hundred Years' War lasted more than one hundred years.
calibration.note: 1337 to 1453, about 116 years.

calibration.statement: Euro banknotes and coins entered circulation before the year 2000.
calibration.note: The euro existed electronically from 1999, but cash arrived in January 2002.

calibration.statement: The Great Wall of China is visible to the unaided eye from the Moon.
calibration.note: It is far too narrow. It is hard to pick out even from low Earth orbit.

calibration.statement: There are more distinct orderings of a standard 52-card deck than there are atoms in the observable universe.
calibration.note: 52 factorial is about 8 x 10^67. Atoms in the observable universe are about 10^80.

calibration.statement: A googol is larger than the number of atoms in the observable universe.
calibration.note: A googol is 10^100, against roughly 10^80 atoms.

calibration.statement: The number of possible chess games exceeds the number of atoms in the observable universe.
calibration.note: The Shannon number is estimated near 10^120.

calibration.statement: The repeating decimal 0.999... is exactly equal to 1.
calibration.note: They are two notations for the same real number, provable several ways.

calibration.statement: It has been proven that every even number greater than two is the sum of two primes.
calibration.note: Goldbach's conjecture is verified far into the large numbers but remains unproven.

calibration.statement: There are infinitely many prime numbers.
calibration.note: Proved by Euclid.

calibration.statement: Pi has been proven to be irrational.
calibration.note: Lambert proved it in 1761.

calibration.statement: In the Monty Hall problem, switching doors wins two-thirds of the time.
calibration.note: Given the standard rules, switching wins whenever the first pick was wrong, which is two times in three.

calibration.statement: There are more atoms in a glass of water than there are glassfuls of water in all the Earth's oceans.
calibration.note: About 10^25 atoms in a glass, against roughly 10^22 glassfuls of ocean.

calibration.statement: The Amazon rainforest supplies about twenty percent of the world's oxygen.
calibration.note: A mature forest consumes nearly as much oxygen as it produces. Its net contribution is close to zero; most atmospheric oxygen came from ocean plankton over geological time.

calibration.statement: Sydney is the capital of Australia.
calibration.note: Canberra is, chosen as a compromise between Sydney and Melbourne.

calibration.statement: Seen from space, the Sun appears yellow.
calibration.note: It is white. Atmospheric scattering removes blue light and makes it look yellow from the ground.

calibration.statement: Chameleons change colour mainly to blend in with their surroundings.
calibration.note: Colour change is driven mostly by temperature regulation and social signalling.

calibration.statement: A penny dropped from the top of the Empire State Building would kill a person it hit on the street.
calibration.note: Its terminal velocity is low and its shape unstable. It would sting.

calibration.statement: Viking warriors wore horned helmets in battle.
calibration.note: No horned helmet has been found in a Viking grave. The image comes from a 19th-century opera design.

calibration.statement: Albert Einstein failed mathematics as a schoolboy.
calibration.note: He had mastered calculus by fifteen. He did fail an entrance exam that covered non-scientific subjects.

calibration.statement: Different regions of the tongue are dedicated to detecting different basic tastes.
calibration.note: The tongue map came from a mistranslated 1901 paper. All taste types are detected across the tongue.

calibration.statement: Mount Fuji is the highest mountain in Asia.
calibration.note: Fuji is about 3,776 m. Everest is about 8,849 m.

calibration.statement: Drinking alcohol raises the body's core temperature in cold conditions.
calibration.note: It dilates surface blood vessels, which feels warm while accelerating heat loss.

calibration.statement: A camel's hump stores water.
calibration.note: The hump stores fat, which is a reserve of energy.

calibration.statement: The Nobel Prizes include a category for mathematics.
calibration.note: There is no mathematics Nobel. The Fields Medal and Abel Prize fill that role.

calibration.statement: The official language of Brazil is Spanish.
calibration.note: It is Portuguese, a result of the 1494 Treaty of Tordesillas.

fermi.prompt: How many piano tuners work in Chicago?
reference: Chicago metro population: about 9 million, so roughly 3 million households.
Say 1 household in 50 owns a piano: about 60,000 household pianos.
Add institutional pianos in schools, churches, bars and halls: call it 10,000 more, so 70,000.
A piano in use gets tuned about once a year: 70,000 tunings a year.
A tuner does 3 to 4 a day, so 800 to 1,000 a year with travel.
70,000 / 900 is roughly 80 full-time tuners.
fermi.answer: About 80 to 200. Trade directories list a few hundred, many of them part time.

fermi.prompt: How many times does a human heart beat in an average lifetime?
reference: Resting rate is about 70 per minute; average 75 across the day to allow for activity.
75 x 60 = 4,500 per hour.
4,500 x 24 = about 108,000 per day.
108,000 x 365 = about 39 million per year.
At 75 years: 39 million x 75 = about 3 billion.
fermi.answer: Roughly 2.5 to 3 billion. Most mammals land within a factor of a few of 1 billion.

fermi.prompt: How many breaths does a person take in a lifetime?
reference: Resting respiration is about 14 per minute; call the daily average 16.
16 x 60 x 24 = about 23,000 breaths per day.
23,000 x 365 = about 8.4 million per year.
Over 75 years: 8.4 million x 75 = about 630 million.
Childhood rates are higher, which nudges the figure up.

fermi.prompt: How many golf balls fit inside a standard school bus?
reference: Bus interior: about 12 m long, 2.4 m wide, 2 m tall = 58 cubic metres.
Subtract seats, wheel wells and engine housing: call the usable space 50 cubic metres.
A golf ball is 4.27 cm across, so its own volume is about 4.1 x 10^-5 cubic metres.
Random packing of spheres fills about 64 percent of space, so each ball claims 6.4 x 10^-5 cubic metres.
fermi.answer: Roughly 500,000 to 900,000. The packing fraction is the step most people forget.

fermi.prompt: How many cells are there in the human body?
reference: Do not average over cell types: one type dominates the count.
Red blood cells run about 5 million per microlitre of blood.
Blood volume is about 5 litres, which is 5 million microlitres.
5 x 10^6 x 5 x 10^6 = 2.5 x 10^13 red blood cells alone.
Red cells are roughly 80 percent of all cells by number, so the total is around 3 x 10^13.
Cross-check by mass: 70 kg at about 1 nanogram per generic cell would give 7 x 10^13, the same order.

fermi.prompt: How many hairs are on a typical human head?
reference: The haired scalp is roughly a cap 30 cm across, so about 700 square centimetres.
Follicle density on the scalp is about 150 to 200 per square centimetre.
fermi.answer: Roughly 100,000 to 150,000. Blond hair runs denser and finer, red hair sparser and thicker.

fermi.prompt: How many grains of sand are on all the beaches of Earth?
reference: A medium grain is about 0.5 mm across, so about 6 x 10^-11 cubic metres; allow for packing gaps and call it 10^-10 cubic metres each.
That gives about 10^10 grains per cubic metre of sand.
World coastline is roughly 350,000 km; say a fifth of it is sandy beach, so 70,000 km, or 7 x 10^7 metres.
Take a beach cross-section 50 m wide and 5 m deep: 250 square metres.
Volume = 7 x 10^7 x 250 = 1.75 x 10^10 cubic metres.
fermi.answer: Around 10^19 to 10^20. Fewer than the stars in the observable universe, which is the usual point of the comparison.

fermi.prompt: How many trees are there on Earth?
reference: Global forest area is about 4 billion hectares, which is 4 x 10^13 square metres.
Tree density in forest varies widely; take 500 stems per hectare as a middling figure.
4 x 10^9 hectares x 500 = 2 x 10^12 trees in forests.
Add savanna, orchards, parks and street trees: call it half again.
Total around 3 x 10^12.
fermi.answer: About 3 trillion. The 2015 Crowther survey put it at 3.04 trillion, which surprised people by being far higher than earlier guesses.

fermi.prompt: How many seconds have elapsed since the year 1 AD?
reference: Elapsed years: about 2,025.
Seconds in a year: 365.25 x 24 x 3,600 = about 3.16 x 10^7.
A useful thing to memorise: pi x 10^7 seconds is close to one year.

fermi.prompt: How much does a typical fair-weather cumulus cloud weigh?
reference: Take a cumulus roughly 1 km on each side: 10^9 cubic metres.
Liquid water content in such a cloud is about 0.5 grams per cubic metre.
10^9 x 0.5 g = 5 x 10^8 grams = 5 x 10^5 kilograms.
That is around 500 tonnes of water, held up by rising air.
fermi.answer: About 500,000 kg. The mass is real; the droplets are just too small to fall fast.

fermi.prompt: What is the total length of all the blood vessels in one human body?
reference: Capillaries dominate the total length; arteries and veins are negligible by comparison.
Estimates of capillary count run from 10^10 to 10^11.
Each capillary is roughly 0.5 to 1 mm long.
Take 4 x 10^10 capillaries at 1 mm: 4 x 10^7 metres = 40,000 km.
The commonly quoted 100,000 km figure assumes a capillary count near 10^11.
fermi.answer: Order of 10^4 to 10^5 km. Enough to wrap the equator at least once.

fermi.prompt: How many pizzas are sold in the United States in one year?
reference: US population is about 335 million.
Say the average person eats pizza once every two weeks: 26 servings a year.
One pizza feeds about three people, so 335 million x 26 / 3 = about 2.9 billion pizzas.
Cross-check from the other side: the US pizza industry turns over roughly 46 billion dollars at maybe 15 dollars a pizza, which is about 3 billion.
Two independent routes agreeing is the strongest signal a Fermi estimate can give you.

fermi.prompt: How many litres of petrol do passenger cars in the United States burn in a year?
reference: Light vehicles in regular use: about 250 million.
Average annual distance: about 19,000 km, which is 12,000 miles.
Fuel economy averages about 10 litres per 100 km, which is roughly 24 miles per gallon.
fermi.answer: About 5 x 10^11 litres, or roughly 130 billion US gallons.

fermi.prompt: How many words does a person speak in a lifetime?
reference: Recording studies put daily speech at about 16,000 words for both men and women.
16,000 x 365 = about 5.8 million words a year.
Assume 72 years of talking after early childhood.
fermi.answer: Around 400 million. The often-repeated claim that women speak three times as many words as men did not survive measurement.

fermi.prompt: How many windows are there in New York City?
reference: NYC has about 3.5 million housing units.
A typical apartment has about 5 windows: 17.5 million residential windows.
Commercial, institutional and industrial buildings add perhaps another 50 percent.
Total around 25 to 30 million.
The classic interview trap here is to start from the population instead of from housing units.

fermi.prompt: How many individual ants are alive on Earth right now?
reference: Earth's land area is about 1.3 x 10^14 square metres.
Much of it is desert, ice or bare rock; call the ant-supporting area 10^14 square metres.
Ground surveys find on the order of 100 ants per square metre in productive habitat, far fewer elsewhere.
Take a weighted average near 150 per square metre over the supporting area.
fermi.answer: About 2 x 10^16, or 20 quadrillion. Their combined mass is comparable to that of all wild birds and mammals together.

fermi.prompt: How much energy is released by a single lightning bolt, in joules?
reference: Charge transferred in a typical flash is about 5 coulombs.
The potential difference between cloud and ground is on the order of 10^8 volts.
Energy = charge x voltage = 5 x 10^8 joules.
Cross-check: that is about 140 kilowatt-hours, roughly what a house uses in a week.
fermi.answer: Order of 10^9 joules. Most of it leaves as heat, light and sound, not as usable electricity.
